The figure summarizes how different monocyte and macrophage populations populate and evolve within an atherosclerotic plaque across the vessel wall. It shows circulating classical monocytes entering from the lumen and from the vasa vasorum, then differentiating into several macrophage states inside the intima. These include inflammatory macrophages, lipid-laden foam cells marked by receptors such as SR-A and CD36, and cavity macrophages. LDL and oxidized lipids drive foam-cell formation, while danger signals activate TLR pathways and inflammatory mediators like IL-1 and TNF.

At the center, the plaque contains a necrotic core beneath a fibrous cap. Cell stress and death release DAMPs, and defective efferocytosis causes dead cells to accumulate, expanding the necrotic core. Some macrophages become efferocytes, but this clearance appears insufficient. A distinct interferon-inducible macrophage population is also shown responding to DAMPs and producing type I interferon.

The diagram also highlights local macrophage proliferation, both in the adventitia and in a MacAIR-like population in the plaque. Non-classical monocytes seem to patrol along the luminal side, while resident adventitial macrophages may derive from embryonic precursors. Overall, the figure emphasizes macrophage heterogeneity, multiple routes of recruitment, and failed clearance as key features of plaque progression.
